content: When a patient is prescribed a daily dose of 25 mg/kg of ethambutol, it is recommended to conduct monthly eye examinations to monitor for potential visual side effects. For patients who have previously undergone antituberculous therapy, administer ethambutol at a dose of 25 mg/kg (11 mg/lb) of body weight as a single oral dose every 24 hours. Concurrently, at least one additional antituberculous drug should be administered, selected based on in vitro susceptibility testing to ensure efficacy. These additional drugs should ideally not have been used previously in the patient’s treatment regimen. After 60 days of therapy, the ethambutol dose should be reduced to 15 mg/kg (7 mg/lb) of body weight, administered as a single oral dose every 24 hours. For adults, the dose of 15 mg/kg per day should be combined with other antituberculous drugs, ensuring the total daily dose does not exceed 1 gram. Ethambutol should not be used as monotherapy, either in initial treatment or retreatment, as it is intended to be used in combination with other anti-TB drugs, such as isoniazid initially, followed by second-line anti-TB drugs if necessary. Ethambutol may reduce the efficacy of the BCG live vaccine due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. It is advised to avoid or use alternative drugs in such cases. Additionally, ethambutol can decrease the effects of allopurinol, febuxostat, and probenecid, potentially leading to hyperuricemia and gout. Dosage adjustments of uric acid-lowering agents may be required. Aluminum hydroxide-containing antacids can increase ethambutol levels by cation binding in the gastrointestinal tract. To minimize this interaction, avoid administering such antacids for at least 4 hours after an ethambutol dose. Ethambutol may cause optic neuritis, which can manifest as decreased visual acuity, color blindness, or other visual defects. These effects are generally reversible upon prompt discontinuation of the drug, although irreversible blindness has been reported in rare cases. Patients with pre-existing visual defects, such as cataracts, recurrent inflammatory eye conditions, optic neuritis, or diabetic retinopathy, may experience difficulty in evaluating changes in visual acuity. In such cases, the potential benefits of treatment should be carefully weighed against the risk of visual deterioration. Liver toxicity, including fatalities, has been reported with ethambutol use. Baseline and periodic hepatic function assessments are recommended. The drug is not recommended for pediatric patients under 13 years of age, as safety conditions for this age group have not been established. Patients with impaired renal function require dosage adjustments based on serum drug levels, as the primary route of excretion is via the kidneys. Ethambutol therapy should be continued until bacteriological conversion is permanent and maximal clinical improvement has been achieved. The drug’s absorption is not significantly affected by food intake. Regular monitoring of organ system functions, including renal, hepatic, and hematopoietic systems, is essential during treatment. Ophthalmologic evaluations, including ophthalmoscopy, finger perimetry, and color discrimination testing, should be performed periodically to detect any adverse effects on vision. During pregnancy, ethambutol should only be used when clearly needed, as it crosses into breast milk. While it is unlikely to harm a nursing infant, caution is advised. Patients with HIV should be aware that breast milk may transmit the virus. Ethambutol is classified as Pregnancy Category B, indicating that controlled studies in pregnant women have shown no evidence of fetal risk. In cases of overdose, immediate medical attention is required. Contact emergency services or a poison control center. Routine laboratory and medical tests, such as sputum tests, eye/vision exams, kidney/liver function tests, and complete blood counts, should be conducted during treatment. Missed doses should be taken as soon as remembered unless it is near the time of the next dose, in which case the missed dose should be skipped. Store ethambutol at room temperature, away from light and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Properly discard expired or unused medication as instructed by a healthcare professional. Ethambutol is used in combination with other medications to treat tuberculosis (TB) and is effective only against bacterial infections. It is not effective for viral infections such as the common cold or flu.
